data.title: What laws or rules apply to civil servants when using information obtained from work?
data.description:
What laws or rules apply to civil servants when using information obtained from work?

Wong Pei Ting
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:00 am UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SINGAPORE – Questions about the laws and rules governing what civil servants can do with information obtained through their work have surfaced recently.

They come after a study claiming they and their relatives disproportionately bought homes near MRT stations that had not yet been publicly announced.

The Public Service Division (PSD) said in its initial response to the paper that it is reviewing the data and methodology and would refer the matter to the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB) if there is "material basis" to do so.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Current rules include annual declarations.

Civil servants have to make declarations of interests in investments and properties to their head of agency every year, as well as when they acquire significant assets, according to a 2024 written parliamentary reply by current Coordinating Minister for Public Services Chan Chun Sing.

ST understands that these declarations could include private residential property, commercial property or any land in Singapore or abroad. The rules could also apply to properties acquired by the public officer's spouse or financially dependent children.

There are also rules stating that officers are not allowed to use privileged information, including information that has not been made public, when buying property for personal gain.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In 2023, then senior minister Teo Chee Hean told Parliament that the Public Service Code of Conduct requires all public officers to take an annual quiz and make declarations including their freedom from financial embarrassment, investments in non-owner-occupied properties and investments in private firms.

He said officers must also make ad hoc declarations when they buy private residential or commercial properties or land.

National University of Singapore corporate governance expert Mak Yuen Teen said the Government should recognise that there are always risks of abuse, regardless of the merits of the working paper.

Pointing to a recent court case involving a former Housing Board group director accused of breaching the agency's database, he said the episode illustrated the need for safeguards.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Regardless of whether we believe the findings are accurate, we should make sure we have safeguards to minimise such risks," he said.

Legislation, codes of conduct that may apply

Some have assumed that the mention of CPIB means that any potential offence highlighted by the study is corruption-related, but lawyers told The Straits Times that the legal implications depend heavily on the circumstances of each case.

Noting that the study does not provide any specific facts for any individuals, lawyers suggested several possible pieces of legislation that could be relevant beyond the Prevention of Corruption Act, as well as internal codes of conduct by which civil servants are bound.

The CPIB is the only agency authorised to investigate corruption offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA), which covers corrupt transactions involving "gratification" – such as money, property, services, favours or other advantages – given or received to induce a person to do something with corrupt intent.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But lawyers said the fact that a civil servant may have used information obtained through work to make a profitable property purchase does not, by itself, establish a corruption offence.

The working paper, authored by four academics based in the US and Hong Kong, claimed that civil servants – in particular those involved in rail planning – disproportionately bought private property near an MRT station, compared with a control group with similar demographics.

It was published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, a US-based non-profit organisation, in September.

Lawyer Gino Singh of Abbots Chambers said the PCA is not an obvious fit based on these facts.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The conventional corruption offences under the Act require corrupt gratification operating as an inducement or reward, he noted. "Here, nobody has offered or given the officer anything. He has simply acted upon information already in his possession," he said.

Benjamin Joshua Ong, an assistant professor of law at Singapore Management University, said merely misusing information for personal gain is not necessarily an offence that the CPIB has the power to investigate.

"The CPIB's main remit is to investigate corruption-related offences. It does have the power to investigate other offences, but only arrestable offences which are disclosed in the course of investigations into corruption-related offences," he told ST.

Professor Walter Woon, a former Attorney-General, said investigations can be conducted by any agency, and CPIB investigations often lead to Penal Code charges.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"What charge might be disclosed is an entirely separate matter. It may not be corruption, but there could be other offences," he said.

Instead of the PCA, lawyers flagged Section 169 of the Penal Code and Section 7(3) of the Public Sector (Governance) Act as possibilities.

Section 169 of the Penal Code states that it is an offence for a public servant who is legally prohibited from buying or bidding for certain property to nonetheless do so. If convicted, a person can be jailed for up to two years, fined, or both, while the property, if purchased, is liable to be confiscated.

Ong said whether this applies depends on whether the civil servant in question was legally bound not to purchase the property, which could come under internal civil service rules that employees are contractually bound to follow.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Section 7(3) states that it is an offence for a relevant public official to use information under the control of a public sector agency and, as a result of that use, obtain a gain for himself or another person, or cause harm or loss to another person. A person can be fined up to $5,000, jailed for up to two years, or both, under this provision.

Lawyers ST spoke to said this Act could be more directly relevant to a scenario involving the use of government information for a private property gain.

But Ong noted that there appear to be no decided cases in which the courts have had an occasion to deal with or interpret Section 7(3), or any other part of the Public Sector (Governance) Act.

Therein lies a possible defence for the civil servant, which is to prove that the information used was "generally available information", he said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Ong said this could cover a possibility raised in several online comments so far – that future MRT stations may be reasonably inferred from the type of construction works being carried out in an area.

Singh said the Official Secrets Act could come into play if an officer told relatives to buy property based on internal knowledge of where an MRT station is going to be announced.

"That is no longer merely an officer privately acting upon information. There has been a communication of official information to another person," he said.

There is a possibility that any wrong behaviour flagged in the study would not fall under the purview of the law but under internal civil service rules, said lawyers.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Singh said a breach of an employment or ethical obligation should not automatically be equated with the commission of a criminal offence.

Ong added that not all the standards explicitly list behaviours that are forbidden. Some take the form of principles and values, which involve an element of judgment.

For example, one of the core principles outlined in the Public Service Code of Conduct is for public officers to be "fair and impartial in carrying out responsibilities, and not be corrupt or seen to be so".

They may also vary in stringency depending on the department.

Ong pointed to rules requiring all public officers to declare visits to local casinos if they visit more than four times a month or purchase an annual pass, while tighter restrictions apply to certain groups of officers.

ST has contacted the PSD and several government agencies involved in transport and land-use planning, including the Land Transport Authority and Urban Redevelopment Authority, for more details on the rules governing property purchases.

Source: The Straits Times © SPH Media Limited. Permission required for reproduction

data.title: Drone owners rush to offload devices ahead of Beijing ban
data.description:
Drone owners rush to offload devices ahead of Beijing ban

Sam DAVIES
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 3:56 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Drone owners in Beijing flocked to designated buy-back sites this week, looking to sell their devices for as much as possible ahead of an impending citywide ban.

New rules in the Chinese capital ban not just the flying of unmanned aerial vehicles but the possession or storage of them, meaning owners have until November 15 to get rid of their drones.

At several authorised buyer sites across the city, AFP witnessed queues of people waiting for staff to appraise their drones and negotiate prices.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

All sites had a visible police presence, indicating the sensitivity of the new laws, and most people there did not want to talk to AFP.

At the flagship store for the world's largest drone maker DJI in Beijing's business district, around a dozen people queued on Thursday morning hoping to sell their drones back for a reasonable price.

Users can sell devices at approved buy-back points and receive a government subsidy of 30 percent of the resale value -- up to a maximum of 3,000 yuan (nearly $450) -- before October 31, and of 15 percent until November 14.

Alternatively, they can recycle them for a subsidy of 200 yuan, or ship them out of Beijing free of charge.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I think (the ban) is reasonable. I can understand why the government wants to ensure safety and manage the airspace," a 48-year-old drone owner surnamed Wu told AFP as he sat in a queue in a DJI store waiting to sell his device.

"After all, Beijing is the capital," said Wu, who bought his drone six years ago for around 6,000 yuan.

He was hoping to get at least 1,000 yuan for the sale, which was what he had been given as a preliminary estimate on the official re-selling app.

Some were not satisfied.

Zhu, 60, who called himself a drone hobbyist, said the buy-back scheme was "robbery".

"It's made me lose a lot of money. This is my private property," he said, adding that he had sold five drones back, losing thousands on the original prices.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Of course I'm not happy... I'm helpless and furious".

Zhu added that the large number of drones being bought back had sent prices plummeting as much as 40 percent.

- Security fears -

Airspace safety fears were raised in June when a light aircraft smashed into Beijing's tallest building, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others -- as well as briefly disrupting the flight path into one of the capital's international airports.

The incident, which was heavily censored, seems to have unsettled Beijing authorities, happening just a few kilometres (miles) from the seat of the Chinese government.

Beijing cited a need to "safeguard the security of the capital" when it announced the complete ban on drone possession inside the city.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Meanwhile, a "low-altitude" expo scheduled to open Thursday in Beijing was abruptly cancelled, with organisers citing control measures from the city government.

Drone owner Wu said he was pleased that the buy-back plan meant he could easily sell his drone -- which he said he no longer used much anyway -- for a reasonable amount.

"I checked some online selling platforms and found that without the subsidy it would sell for maybe half the price", he said.

It is difficult to know how many drones will be affected by the move.

There were 3.285 million drones registered nationwide at the end of 2025, according to the Civil Aviation Administration, but it is not necessary to register drone ownership in most of the country.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Online, many Beijingers posted farewells to their drone collections.

"There's nothing I can do, thanks for your company," wrote one user on social media platform Xiaohongshu, known as RedNote abroad.

"I hope you can keep roaming the skies in the future."

data.title: US appeals court rejects Trump policy allowing swift deportations to third countries
data.description:
US appeals court rejects Trump policy allowing swift deportations to third countries

By Nate Raymond
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 3:50 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Nate Raymond

BOSTON, Sept 18 (Reuters) - A US federal appeals court rejected on Friday a policy adopted by the Trump administration that allows authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety ‌concerns.

Ruling in a case that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel of the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court ‌of Appeals largely upheld a February decision by a lower-court judge that declared the Department of Homeland Security's policy unlawful.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by migrants subject to ​deportation orders that has become a key test of what due-process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.

"This decision confirms that due process and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented by putting someone on a plane to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings," Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said.

Under President Donald Trump, the administration has ‌entered into a series of agreements that have ⁠allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The government is expected to appeal. Earlier ⁠in the case, the administration twice convinced the Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants' due-process rights, clearing the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The administration has also carried out third-country deportations of people to nations including Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia and the Central African Republic.

DHS General Counsel James Percival ​posted on ​X that the policy remains in force because the 1st Circuit's decision is not ​yet in effect.

"If you claim fear in your home country, ‌DHS has the right to send you elsewhere," he said.

THIRD-COUNTRY DEPORTATIONS

In March 2025, DHS adopted a policy aimed at addressing individuals who were subject to final orders of deportation but had been granted protections in immigration court against being sent back to their countries of origin.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The policy would allow migrants to be sent to alternative countries if immigration authorities have credible diplomatic assurances they will not be persecuted or tortured there.

The policy called for only minimal notice before a migrant could be sent to a third country that had not given the State Department such assurances.

US District Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of Democratic ‌President Joe Biden, set aside the policy and concluded that it failed to protect ​migrants' due-process rights and could lead to their swift deportation to unfamiliar and potentially dangerous ​countries, without notice.

On appeal, the Trump administration contended that Murphy's order, ​if left intact, would usurp its authority to execute potentially thousands of valid orders of deportation to third countries.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But US ‌Circuit Judge Seth Aframe, writing for Friday's panel, said Murphy ​adopted a "sensible" interpretation of the immigration law ​requiring migrants be given a "meaningful" chance to raise any concerns before they are deported.

"DHS's proposed interpretation would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of noncitizens who are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination," Aframe wrote. "We decline to adopt such ​an interpretation."

The panel included two Biden appointees, including Aframe, ‌and a judge appointed by a Republican president.

However, the 1st Circuit overturned one part of Murphy's ruling on procedural grounds. It ​concerned whether the government must first try to deport migrants to countries they have ties to before sending them to third ​countries.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani and William Mallard)

data.title: Trump says Denmark to give US 'permanent control' over Greenland security
data.description:
Trump says Denmark to give US 'permanent control' over Greenland security

Danny KEMP
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 3:12 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had struck a deal with Denmark to give Washington "permanent control" over Greenland's security that would bar Russia and China from setting up bases in the Arctic territory.

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.

Denmark and Greenland -- an autonomous territory controlled by Copenhagen -- both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But the terms of the deal remain uncertain, and Denmark maintains its sovereignty remains intact.

In a statement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the deal as "an agreement which at the same time recognizes the sovereignty an territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination."

"I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

"From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The 80-year-old said it was an "'Infinite Life' Agreement, there is no end!" and said Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory.

- 'Good agreement' -

Trump has repeatedly warned about Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland as a strategic battle for supremacy in a warming Arctic unfolds, and the State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so.

"This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors," a State Department official said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

At the Davos economic forum this past January, Trump reached a purported deal with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte over the future of Greenland, the terms of which have remained vague.

Frederiksen had said Monday that she was "optimistic" that ongoing discussions with the United States and Greenland since January could resolve the dispute.

She said Friday she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," adding that it was "good for NATO and Europe."

Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the United States "strengthens" the territory's security.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- NATO tensions -

Trump gave no details about how the deal would work, and it was not clear if it was linked to or substantially different from the Rutte deal.

But several media outlets have reported that the United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.

A 1951 defense pact, updated in 2004, already allows Washington to ramp up troop deployments and military installations on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance.

At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.

Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

data.title: South Korea justice nominee withdraws in Lee's second cabinet setback as polls slide
data.description:
South Korea justice nominee withdraws in Lee's second cabinet setback as polls slide

Reuters
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 3:06 am UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

FILE PHOTO: South Korea's parliament holds nomination hearing for new justice minister

1 of 3
FILE PHOTO: South Korean Justice Minister nominee Kim Seung-won speaks during his confirmation hearing at the National Assembly in Seoul, South Korea, September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Kim Hong-Ji/File Photo

SEOUL, Sept 19 (Reuters) - South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's nominee for justice minister ‌withdrew from consideration on Saturday, the second ‌of Lee's cabinet picks to step aside this month as ​his approval ratings slump.

Kim Seung-won's exit follows the withdrawal of Yong Hye-in as nominee for gender-equality minister on Sunday, in the latest fallout from ‌Lee's cabinet reshuffle ⁠in late August.

Kim, who said he did not want to add any burden ⁠to Lee's administration, criticised a conservative lawmaker who had accused him of lobbying regulators over a ​drug trial ​and of financial ​irregularities. Kim has denied ‌the allegations.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I gravely accept that I did not meet the public's expectations, and I will deeply reflect on my shortcomings," Kim told a press conference.

A Gallup Korea poll released on Friday put ‌Lee's public approval at ​37%, the lowest since he ​took office in ​June 2025, a decline pollsters have ‌partly linked to criticism over ​his personnel ​appointments.

At a press conference on Friday, Lee acknowledged shortcomings in his administration's screening of nominees. "We ​are currently ‌working to reexamine our personnel system," the ​president said.

(Reporting by Joyce Lee in Seoul; ​Editing by William Mallard)

data.title: Indigenous, civil-society groups sue Prabowo over forest fire response
data.description:
Indigenous, civil-society groups sue Prabowo over forest fire response

Reuters
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 2:58 am UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Wildfires in West Kalimantan province

1 of 3
A staff member of the Regional Disaster Agency (BPBD) sprays water to extinguish a fire in a peatland area burnt by wildfires, in Kubu Raya, West Kalimantan province, Indonesia, September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana

JAKARTA, Sept 19 (Reuters) - A group of indigenous and civil-society organisations in Indonesia's West Kalimantan has filed a ‌class-action lawsuit against President Prabowo Subianto and other ‌authorities over their handling of forest fires in the region, its lawyer said ​on Saturday.

Below are more details:

• The case was registered at the Pontianak court in West Kalimantan with the first hearing scheduled for October 7, the court filing shows.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

• "This lawsuit was filed ‌in response to the ⁠West Kalimantan public's concerns over the government's negligence and failure to prevent and tackle forest and ⁠land fires that recur every year," Glorio Sanen, the plaintiffs' lawyer told Reuters on Saturday.

• The presidential office did not ​immediately respond ​to request for comment.

• The ​plaintiffs are West Kalimantan chapter ‌of the Indigenous Peoples Alliance of the Archipelago, West Kalimantan branch of Catholic Youth, Perkumpulan Laman Punyung Indonesia and an individual, Sisilius Rami, the filing shows.

• Indonesia is battling its most intense wildfires in 11 years and the government has ‌warned that the fires could continue ​until November this year.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

• In 2016, ​a lawsuit was brought ​by seven Indonesian residents against then-President Joko Widodo, ‌his cabinet ministers and local ​governments over their ​handling of forest fires in 2015.

• After initially winning at the district court, the decision on 2016's lawsuit ​was overturned when ‌the Supreme Court granted the government's petition for judicial ​review in 2022, according to media reports.

(Reporting by Stefanno ​Sulaiman; Editing by Sam Holmes)

data.title: 'DISGUSTING and FAKE': Hegseth Rages Over New Report On U.S. Military Casualties
data.description:
'DISGUSTING and FAKE': Hegseth Rages Over New Report On U.S. Military Casualties

Anthony Orrico
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 2:23 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth lashed out on social media Friday following a report from The Washington Post that found more U.S. service members had died in the Middle East during the war with Iran than the Pentagon had disclosed publicly. 

"This is DISGUSTING and FAKE. A complete LIE," wrote Hegseth on X. "Shame on the Washington Post — they're worse than Iranian state media."

Politics: Workers Are Falling Behind Due To Trump's War-Induced Inflation

While Hegseth responded on social media, the Pentagon declined to answer the Post's questions about discrepancies in the casualty count. 

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Post's report found there have been at least 22 military fatalities since the U.S. and Israel launched the war in Iran on Feb. 28. That number is four higher than what appears in the Pentagon's official Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS. 

The report cited five U.S. officials who spoke with the Post on the condition of anonymity. 

However, a sixth official said the casualty count could be as high as 23. The report noted that not all the deaths were tied directly to the conflict, but all were U.S. personnel in the Middle East. 

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Hegseth has faced growing scrutiny over the conflict, even having articles of impeachment introduced against him this week by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). 

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Massie, in his resolution, accuses Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors related to the Trump administration launching the war with Iran without congressional approval and military strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean. 

Politics: Trump Reportedly Fumes At Hegseth Over Military's Missile Shortage

However, after House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent members home early on Wednesday, Massie's resolution to impeach Hegseth and his push to release more files related to the Jeffrey Epstein investigation will not be voted on until after the midterm elections, if at all. 

"We're calling off Congress? And we're in the majority?" Massie said on the House floor Wednesday. 

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I'm trying to get justice for the Epstein survivors," he said. "I'm trying to stop a war."

Johnson labeled Massie's attempt to impeach Hegseth a "stunt." 

"Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War," Johnson said.

data.title: Sikh truck driver stabbed 17 times in unprovoked Wyoming attack raises fears of assaults against South Asians, officials say
data.description:
Sikh truck driver stabbed 17 times in unprovoked Wyoming attack raises fears of assaults against South Asians, officials say

Eduardo Cuevas, Jeff Winter, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 1:32 am UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A Sikh truck driver was stabbed more than a dozen times in an unprovoked attack by a man at a Wyoming rest stop, according to local officials, raising an alarm among Asian American advocates who are warning about inflammatory rhetoric against South Asian truckers.

Officials have not yet determined the suspect's motive, and it's unclear whether the incident is being investigated as a hate crime. The victim's lawyer has called for a thorough investigation into "any potential hate-crime or civil-rights dimension of this attack."

Early Sunday morning, the truck driver, identified by his attorney only as Singh, had stopped at a rest area along I-80 in Sweetwater County when he was followed into the bathroom by a man later identified as Andrew Bzdak, according to the sheriff's office. Inside the men's room, Bzdak allegedly attacked Singh from behind, stabbing him 17 times with a knife, including twice in the neck and twice in the chest, according to an arrest warrant.

After the attack, Singh ran out of the bathroom and was later seen on video lying on the ground in the parking lot, according to CNN affiliate KOVR. Records show Singh had called emergency services and said he'd been stabbed multiple times. Responding officers saw "large amounts of blood" inside the men's room, the bathroom lobby, outside the building and by a parked semi-truck, the records show.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Singh was airlifted to the Wyoming Medical Center in Casper, according to the warrant for Bzdak's arrest. He continues to recover from his injuries, according to a Friday update from Jasjit Singh, director of legal services at the Jakara Movement, a California-based advocacy organization serving Punjabi Sikhs and representing the truck driver.

The neighboring Carbon County Sheriff's Office later detained Bzdak after he allegedly fled the scene in his own truck, according to court records. A family who had heard Singh's screams inside the rest stop bathroom followed Bzdak eastbound on I-80 and called police to report the incident, officials said.

Bzdak, 44, is charged with one count of attempting to commit first-degree murder, according to court records. CNN has reached out to the state public defender's office, which is representing Bzdak, and the Sweetwater County Attorney's Office for comment.

Jasjit Singh said there has yet to be a public determination that the "extraordinarily violent attack" was bias-motivated because of the victim's identity as a Punjabi Sikh. Bzdak is White, the county attorney's office said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Now you have this additional fear that, as a South Asian or Punjabi Sikh truck driver, you have to deal with these fears that you may be attacked for how you look," Jasjit Singh told KOVR.

Some advocates have cited recent social media posts by the Department of Homeland Security, including one with an AI-generated graphic of a South Asian man and a tagline saying "Get off our roads, you don't know how to drive Mr. Singh" as fueling such attacks. DHS later deleted the post.

In a statement to CNN about Sunday's stabbing, a DHS spokesperson said any attempts to blame the agency "for an unrelated attack is RECKLESS and FALSE. We will not speculate on motives."

The North American Punjabi Trucking Association, an advocacy nonprofit, called DHS' post "disgraceful, disrespectful, and deeply troubling." The association acknowledged concerns raised by DHS around fraud with commercial driver's licenses, unqualified drivers and English language proficiency.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

However, in a social media post, the association said, "Using the name 'Mr. Singh,' portraying a South Asian man as someone who 'doesn't know how to drive,' and pairing that imagery with 'America for Americans' sends a message far beyond enforcement. It risks turning a legitimate safety issue into a stereotype aimed at Punjabi, Sikh, South Asian, and immigrant truck drivers."

About one in five US truck drivers are Sikh, according to the North American Punjabi Trucking Association, though there are no official estimates, The Associated Press reported.

On Thursday, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL), who is Indian American, said the stabbing of Singh came amid "rising hatred targeting Sikh and South Asian Americans," including from the DHS. "Those who turn it into violence must be held accountable," Krishnamoorthi said in a social media post. "And all of us need to stand together against both. America must be better than this."

Bzdak is being held on a $1 million bond in the Sweetwater County Detention Center.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

He has a criminal history in California dating back to 2004, including convictions of assault with a deadly weapon, drunk driving and vandalism, California court records show.

Bzdak has a preliminary hearing set for September 24 in circuit court.

CNN's Laura Sharman contributed to this report.

data.title: 'Pause' on overt repression in Venezuela, but reforms still needed: HRW
data.description:
'Pause' on overt repression in Venezuela, but reforms still needed: HRW

AFP News
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 1:38 am UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez has overseen a "pause" in the overt repression of opponents since taking office in January, Human Rights Watch (HRW) said Friday, 18 years after the organization was expelled from the country.

Speaking after a meeting with Rodriguez, HRW said that Venezuelan activists, opposition leaders and journalists reported being "much freer to carry out their work" but said securing the gains required "robust institutional reforms and the release of all political prisoners."

Rodriguez's talks Thursday with HRW representatives was seen as a key moment in Venezuela's transition from the hardline socialist rule of ex-president Nicolas Maduro.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The New York-based rights group was thrown out of Venezuela in 2008 by Maduro's mentor and predecessor, the leftist revolutionary Hugo Chavez.

Maduro himself oversaw an increasingly authoritarian government, marked by two reelections widely dismissed as fraudulent.

He was captured by US forces in Caracas in January and flown to New York to face trial.

Since taking over, Rodriguez has pushed through a sweeping amnesty, released hundreds of political prisoners and closed the notorious El Helicoide detention center, where rights groups say inmates were tortured.

Her government has also announced plans to reform the judiciary and on Thursday unblocked some news sites that had been censored for years.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

HRW said during its visit to Venezuela this week that its representatives had met with government critics who had come out of hiding after more than a year or dared report the arbitrary arrest of a loved one for the first time.

But it noted that at least 344 political prisoners remain behind bars, according to the count of a leading Venezuelan human rights group. and that many more remain under house arrest.

The organization also cited accounts of prisoners still being mistreated and urged the closure of another notorious prison, Rodeo 1.

- Call for free, fair elections -

The HRW team's visit to Venezuela came days before Rodriguez is expected to travel to New York to attend the UN General Assembly, a major step towards ending Venezuela's isolation on the world stage.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Some critics argue that with former Maduro loyalists still running the show, alongside the support of US President Donald Trump's administration, Venezuela cannot move on from its repressive past.

HRW noted that Washington had "focused largely on advancing the Trump administration's economic goals" in Venezuela since Maduro's ouster.

It called on Washington to "use its leverage to play a leading role in pushing for meaningful human rights change."

On Thursday, the interim government in Caracas began a new round of negotiations with an opposition faction on a political transition.

HRW echoed the opposition's calls for "timely, free, and fair elections."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"That urgently requires allowing political opponents to participate in the political process and run for public office," said Federico Borello, HRW deputy executive director.

"We know that the legislative and institutional apparatus of the last 27 years remains intact," he added.

The unexpected meeting between Rodriguez and HRW on Thursday was preceded by an announcement that dozens of news websites that had been censored in Venezuela for years were being unblocked.

Additionally, political dialogue with the opposition has resumed, with stated aims of improving freedom of expression and supporting a political transition post-Maduro.

The US-backed negotiations began in August, and a second round of talks is expected to conclude September 23.

data.title: 2 weeks after the end of Lindsay Clancy’s trial, the holdout juror comes forward and Patrick Clancy speaks out
data.description:
2 weeks after the end of Lindsay Clancy’s trial, the holdout juror comes forward and Patrick Clancy speaks out

Nicki Brown, Alex Stambaugh, Alisha Ebrahimji, Rebekah Riess, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 1:01 am UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Two weeks after the triple-murder trial of Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial, new voices, including the lone holdout juror and Lindsay's ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, are coming forward to speak out about the case.

The lone holdout juror in the trial – accused of having an "agenda" by Clancy's defense attorney after the seven-week trial ended without a verdict – said in a statement Thursday his views on the Massachusetts mother were misrepresented by his fellow jurors.

"I didn't have any doubts," Michael Péguy Desronvil said in his statement. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Boston Globe said this week it confirmed the identity of Desronvil, 48, through photos published online, court records and an interview with one of his fellow jurors.

The mistrial left Clancy's future uncertain, as prosecutors have not yet decided whether to pursue a new trial.

In an extraordinary note to the judge on the sixth day of deliberations, the jury foreperson – later identified as Roni Carlson – said Desronvil "has made statements acknowledging doubt, but refuses to apply it to the verdict as the law states," prompting an unsuccessful request from Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington to have the juror replaced by an alternate.

But in his new statement, Desronvil says he felt all along the evidence pointed to a guilty verdict.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned," he said in the statement.

The judge in the case declared a mistrial on September 4 after the jury repeatedly said it couldn't reach a unanimous verdict. Clancy's lawyer argued she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children – Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months – at the family's Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023.

"There's one juror who refuses to listen to the law that you've given him or her on reasonable doubt," Reddington told the judge in his attempt to have the juror removed.

Since the mistrial was declared, several other jurors who were leaning toward finding Clancy not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility have given interviews describing frustrating conversations inside the deliberation room.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"There was times he wouldn't engage, like he'd be scrolling on his phone while people were talking to him, things like that," juror Nick Dargie told ABC News.

"He had the hardest time getting off the fact that Lindsay viciously killed her children," juror Kellie Farina told NBC10 Boston.

During the weekslong trial, Clancy acknowledged she killed her three children, but her lawyers argued she should not be held criminally responsible because she was in the midst of a psychotic episode when she fatally strangled them and attempted suicide.

The panel, comprised of nine women and three men, was unable to reach a unanimous verdict after more than 38 hours of deliberations. The jurors sent notes to the court indicating they were split 11 to 1, with the majority at one point alleging the lone holdout was unable to follow the law on reasonable doubt. The judge ultimately declared a mistrial.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Carlson told NBC10 there was no doubt Clancy killed her children, but said it was also obvious to jurors that she loved them.

The Plymouth County District Attorney's Office previously declined to comment on reports about the juror identities. Clancy is due back in court for a hearing on September 29 as prosecutors determine whether to seek a retrial.

In a statement on X, lawyer Edward Andrew Paltzik said he was representing the holdout juror, writing "please pray for him and help us protect him," without identifying the man.

"He is presently safe and sound at an undisclosed secure location in a rural area of Northern New England," Paltzik wrote.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Rest assured that the evil people who have so viciously attacked this American Hero and Champion of Justice will be held accountable to the maximum extent of the law and beyond," the statement added, describing the man as a devoted father and man of God.

CNN has reached out to Paltzik for more information and whether any legal action is being taken on behalf of the juror.

"There will be a time for accountability and a time for the real story of the Lindsay Clancy Trial to be told. But not right now," Paltzik said in a second post early Friday, adding neither he nor his client would be giving interviews.

"Any attempts to contact our Heroic Lone Holdout Juror will not be well-taken. Please respect his dignity, humanity, and privacy. Stay away from his home, stop calling him, and don't even think about deciphering his location," Paltzik wrote. "We look forward to sharing more information in the coming days on an appropriate timeline, including all of the ways in which you can support this incredible and unique man, and the cause of truth and justice that he so righteously stands for."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"On behalf of our American Hero and Champion of Justice, thank you to all the patriotic Americans who have stood in solidarity behind him with such deeply touching generosity, kindness, and warmth," he concluded.

Clancy's ex-husband sits down with '60 Minutes'

Also coming forward following the end of the closely watched trial, is her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy. He and his new wife sat down for an interview with CBS' "60 Minutes," which will air on Sunday.

unknown content item

-

Patrick Clancy had been the first witness called to testify in the triple-murder trial of his ex-wife. He spent two days testifying about Lindsay's downward spiral that culminated in the deaths of their three children.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In his interview, Clancy told CBS correspondent Ross Douthat he still talks to his kids "all the time."

Asked by Douthat whether he feels angry at himself, Clancy said: "I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time, and I live with the outcome."

"I live with it every day, but I think I did the best I could," he repeated.

Dr. Rachel Danis, a fertility doctor in New York City, married Patrick Clancy in April, CBS reported. During the course of Lindsay's trial, both Patrick and Danis became subjects of unfounded conspiracy theories.

Lawyers for Patrick recently announced they will take legal action to stop the barrage of online conspiracy theorists.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

unknown content item

-

Danis joined her husband for his interview with "60 Minutes." "I don't understand how this story has been so twisted," she said in the interview. "But I would hope people know that Pat is, as I said before, the most selfless father and supportive partner, and I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday, and I don't think there's anything wrong with that."

CNN's Eric Levenson, Cindy Von Quednow and Isa Mudannayake contributed to this report.
